HHS’s 2024 HIPAA Security Rule NPRM would have changed the post-2013 Omnibus Security Rule from a relatively flexible, risk-based framework into a much more prescriptive cybersecurity rule. The 2013 Omnibus Rule made business associates directly subject to the Security Rule, but it left the core structure of “required” versus “addressable” implementation specifications, flexible implementation, and broad safeguard standards largely intact. See 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.302, 164.306, 164.308, 164.310, 164.312, 164.314, 164.316; 78 Fed. Reg. 5566, 5693–95 (Jan. 25, 2013).

The 2024 NPRM was released by HHS OCR on Dec. 27, 2024 and published as **“HIPAA Security Rule To Strengthen the Cybersecurity of Electronic Protected Health Information,” 90 Fed. Reg. 898 (Jan. 6, 2025)**: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/06/2024-30983/hipaa-security-rule-to-strengthen-the-cybersecurity-of-electronic-protected-health-information. HHS’s summary is also at: https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/hipaa-security-rule-nprm/factsheet/index.html.

| Area | Rule after 2013 Omnibus | 2024 NPRM proposed change |
|---|---|---|
| **Required vs. addressable safeguards** | The Security Rule distinguished “required” and “addressable” implementation specifications; required specs had to be implemented, while addressable specs required an assessment of whether they were reasonable and appropriate. 45 C.F.R. § 164.306(d). | HHS proposed eliminating the required/addressable distinction and making implementation specifications mandatory, subject only to limited exceptions. Proposed revisions to 45 C.F.R. § 164.306; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Risk analysis** | Entities had to conduct an “accurate and thorough assessment” of potential risks and vulnerabilities to ePHI. 45 C.F.R. § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A). | HHS proposed much more specific risk-analysis content: written risk analysis, review of technology asset inventory and network map, identification of threats, vulnerabilities, predisposing conditions, and risk levels based on likelihood and impact. Proposed revisions to 45 C.F.R. § 164.308; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Asset inventory and network map** | The existing rule did not expressly require a technology asset inventory or network map; it required general risk analysis, information-system activity review, and documentation. 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.308(a)(1), 164.316. | HHS proposed requiring a written technology asset inventory and network map showing movement of ePHI through electronic information systems, reviewed and updated at least annually and after material changes. Proposed 45 C.F.R. § 164.308; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Encryption** | Encryption of stored ePHI was “addressable” under access controls, and encryption of transmitted ePHI was also “addressable.” 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.312(a)(2)(iv), 164.312(e)(2)(ii). | HHS proposed requiring encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit, with limited exceptions. Proposed 45 C.F.R. § 164.312; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Multi-factor authentication** | The rule required unique user identification and person/entity authentication, but did not expressly require MFA. 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.312(a)(2)(i), 164.312(d). | HHS proposed requiring multi-factor authentication for access to relevant electronic information systems, with limited exceptions. Proposed 45 C.F.R. § 164.312; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Vulnerability management and penetration testing** | The existing rule required risk management, information-system activity review, and periodic technical/nontechnical evaluation, but did not specify vulnerability-scan or penetration-test intervals. 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B), 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D), 164.308(a)(8). | HHS proposed requiring vulnerability scanning at least every six months and penetration testing at least annually. Proposed 45 C.F.R. § 164.308; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Security incident response** | Entities had to identify and respond to suspected or known security incidents, mitigate harmful effects, and document incidents and outcomes. 45 C.F.R. § 164.308(a)(6). | HHS proposed more prescriptive written security-incident-response plans and procedures, testing, and related documentation requirements. Proposed 45 C.F.R. § 164.308; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Contingency planning / resilience** | The rule required data backup plans, disaster recovery plans, and emergency-mode operation plans; testing and criticality analysis were addressable. 45 C.F.R. § 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A)–(E). | HHS proposed strengthening contingency planning, including written procedures to restore certain relevant electronic information systems and data within 72 hours, annual testing, and more specific backup/recovery obligations. Proposed 45 C.F.R. § 164.308; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Network segmentation and anti-malware** | The current technical safeguards require access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, authentication, and transmission security, but do not expressly mandate network segmentation or anti-malware controls. 45 C.F.R. § 164.312. | HHS proposed requiring network segmentation and anti-malware protections as specific cybersecurity controls. Proposed 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.308, 164.312; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Documentation** | Entities had to maintain Security Rule policies, procedures, and required documentation for six years and update documentation as needed. 45 C.F.R. § 164.316(b). | HHS proposed requiring written documentation of essentially all Security Rule policies, procedures, plans, analyses, assessments, and implementation activities in more specific form. Proposed 45 C.F.R. § 164.316; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Business associates and subcontractors** | After Omnibus, business associates had to comply with applicable Security Rule requirements; BA contracts had to require compliance, subcontractor flow-downs, and security-incident reporting. 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.302, 164.308(b), 164.314(a)(2). | HHS proposed requiring stronger assurances from business associates, including annual verification/certification that required technical safeguards are in place and notice to covered entities of contingency-plan activation without unreasonable delay and within 24 hours. Proposed 45 C.F.R. § 164.314; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Access termination / workforce changes** | The existing workforce-security and access-management standards required authorization, supervision, clearance, termination, and access-establishment/modification procedures, several of which were addressable. 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.308(a)(3), 164.308(a)(4). | HHS proposed more specific timing and notification duties when workforce access to ePHI or relevant electronic information systems is changed or terminated. Proposed 45 C.F.R. § 164.308; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |
| **Compliance audits** | The existing rule required periodic evaluation in response to environmental or operational changes, but did not expressly require an annual compliance audit. 45 C.F.R. § 164.308(a)(8). | HHS proposed requiring covered entities and business associates to conduct compliance audits at least annually. Proposed 45 C.F.R. § 164.308; 90 Fed. Reg. 898. |

**Bottom line:** after the 2013 Omnibus Rule, HIPAA Security Rule compliance remained built around flexible, scalable administrative, physical, and technical safeguards, with many “addressable” specifications. 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.306–164.316. The 2024 NPRM proposed to make the rule substantially more prescriptive by mandating concrete cybersecurity practices—asset inventories, network maps, encryption, MFA, vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, network segmentation, stronger contingency planning, annual audits, and stronger business-associate verification obligations. 90 Fed. Reg. 898; proposed revisions to 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.306, 164.308, 164.310, 164.312, 164.314, 164.316.

**164.304 Definitions.**
§ 164.304 Definitions.
  ----------------------

As used in this subpart, the following terms have the following meanings:

Access means the ability or the means necessary to read, write, modify, or communicate data/information or otherwise use any system resource. (This definition applies to “access” as used in this subpart, not as used in subparts D or E of this part.)

Administrative safeguards are administrative actions, and policies and procedures, to manage the selection, development, implementation, and maintenance of security measures to protect electronic protected health information and to manage the conduct of the covered entity's or business associate's workforce in relation to the protection of that information.

Authentication means the corroboration that a person is the one claimed.

Availability means the property that data or information is accessible and useable upon demand by an authorized person.

Confidentiality means the property that data or information is not made available or disclosed to unauthorized persons or processes.

Encryption means the use of an algorithmic process to transform data into a form in which there is a low probability of assigning meaning without use of a confidential process or key.

Facility means the physical premises and the interior and exterior of a building(s).

Information system means an interconnected set of information resources under the same direct management control that shares common functionality. A system normally includes hardware, software, information, data, applications, communications, and people.

Integrity means the property that data or information have not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.

Malicious software means software, for example, a virus, designed to damage or disrupt a system.

Password means confidential authentication information composed of a string of characters.

Physical safeguards are physical measures, policies, and procedures to protect a covered entity's or business associate's electronic information systems and related buildings and equipment, from natural and environmental hazards, and unauthorized intrusion.

Security or Security measures encompass all of the administrative, physical, and technical safeguards in an information system.

Security incident means the attempted or successful unauthorized access, use, disclosure, modification, or destruction of information or interference with system operations in an information system.

Technical safeguards means the technology and the policy and procedures for its use that protect electronic protected health information and control access to it.

User means a person or entity with authorized access.

A covered entity or business associate must, in accordance with § 164.306:

(iii) Access control and validation procedures (Addressable). Implement procedures to control and validate a person's access to facilities based on their role or function, including visitor control, and control of access to software programs for testing and revision.

(iv) Maintenance records (Addressable). Implement policies and procedures to document repairs and modifications to the physical components of a facility which are related to security (for example, hardware, walls, doors, and locks).

(b) Standard: Workstation use. (d)(1) Standard: Device and media controls. Implement policies and procedures that govern the receipt and removal of hardware and electronic media that contain electronic protected health information into and out of a facility, and the movement of these items within the facility.

question.question: What's the substantive difference between NIST AI RMF 1.0 (January 2023) and the earlier 2022 working drafts in terms of trustworthiness characteristics?
question.expected_answer: The final NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023) consolidated the trustworthiness characteristics into a set of seven: valid & reliable; safe; secure & resilient; accountable & transparent; explainable & interpretable; privacy-enhanced; and fair (with managed harmful bias). Earlier 2022 drafts treated these as a longer overlapping list with terms like 'enhanced privacy' and 'bias mitigation' that were renamed for clarity, and the GOVERN function was strengthened relative to drafts to emphasise organisation-wide responsibility rather than only the AI team.

output.answer:
The substantive change is **not that NIST invented an entirely new trustworthiness model in January 2023**, but that AI RMF 1.0 **consolidated and reframed** the earlier 2022 draft concepts into a cleaner set of seven “trustworthy AI characteristics,” with clearer relationships among them.

### 1. Draft 1 used a three-part taxonomy; AI RMF 1.0 uses seven integrated characteristics

In the **March 2022 Initial Draft**, NIST organized trustworthiness into three buckets:

- **Technical characteristics**: accuracy, reliability, robustness, and resilience or ML security.  
  *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.1, Table of Contents and §5.1.3–5.1.4.*
- **Socio-technical characteristics**: explainability, interpretability, privacy, safety, and managing bias.  
  *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.2 and Table of Contents.*
- **Guiding principles**: fairness, accountability, and transparency.  
  *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.3.*

By contrast, **AI RMF 1.0** presents a unified set of seven characteristics:

1. Valid and Reliable  
2. Safe  
3. Secure and Resilient  
4. Accountable and Transparent  
5. Explainable and Interpretable  
6. Privacy-Enhanced  
7. Fair — with Harmful Bias Managed  

*NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.1–§3.7; Fig. 4.*

So the main structural difference is that **fairness, accountability, and transparency moved from “guiding principles” into the core trustworthiness characteristics**, and “bias management” became part of the fairness characteristic rather than a separate socio-technical item. *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.2.5 and §5.3; NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.4 and §3.7.*

### 2. “Accuracy” and “robustness” were absorbed into “Valid and Reliable”

The 2022 drafts treated **accuracy, reliability, and robustness** more explicitly as separate technical ideas. Draft 2’s “Valid and Reliable” section still said accuracy and robustness are interdependent factors contributing to validity and trustworthiness. *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.1.*

In AI RMF 1.0, the headline characteristic is **“Valid and Reliable.”** Validation is defined as confirmation that requirements for a specific intended use have been fulfilled, and reliability is the ability to perform as required over time under given conditions. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.1.* Figure 4 also makes **Valid & Reliable the base condition** for other trustworthiness characteristics. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, Fig. 4.*

Substantively, this means the final RMF treats accuracy and robustness less as standalone trustworthiness labels and more as parts of a broader lifecycle concept: whether the system is valid for its intended context and reliable over time. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.1; NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.1.*

### 3. “Resilience or ML security” became “Secure and Resilient”

Draft 1 used the label **“Resilience or ML Security”** and described resilience/security as the ability to withstand adversarial attacks or unexpected environmental or usage changes. *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.1.4.*

AI RMF 1.0 separates and clarifies the concepts under **“Secure and Resilient.”** It says resilient AI can withstand unexpected adverse events or changes and degrade safely and gracefully when necessary, while secure AI maintains confidentiality, integrity, and availability through protection mechanisms preventing unauthorized access and use. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.3.* It also states that security and resilience are related but distinct: resilience is the ability to return to normal function after adverse events, while security includes protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover from attacks. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.3.*

So the substantive difference is greater precision: the final version no longer treats ML security and resilience as almost interchangeable. *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.1.4; NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.3.*

### 4. “Transparent and Accountable” became “Accountable and Transparent”

Draft 2 used **“Transparent and Accountable.”** It emphasized transparency as information availability about the AI system and described accountability in terms of responsible parties when risky outcomes occur. *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.5.*

AI RMF 1.0 reverses the formulation to **“Accountable and Transparent.”** It states that trustworthy AI depends upon accountability and that accountability presupposes transparency. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.4.* Figure 4 also depicts **Accountable & Transparent as cross-cutting**, relating to all other characteristics. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, Fig. 4.*

That is a substantive emphasis shift: final AI RMF 1.0 makes accountability the governance-oriented anchor, with transparency as a necessary enabler. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.4 and Fig. 4; NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.5.*

### 5. “Bias is managed” became “harmful bias managed”

Draft 1 had a separate socio-technical characteristic called **“Managing Bias,”** and it discussed systemic, computational, and human bias. *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.2.5.* Draft 2 used the label **“Fair – and Bias Is Managed.”** *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.3.*

AI RMF 1.0 changes the final label to **“Fair – with Harmful Bias Managed.”** *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.7.* That wording matters: it recognizes that not every bias is necessarily harmful, while fairness requires attention to equality, equity, discrimination, accessibility, and contextual harms. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.7.*

So the final version narrows the risk-management target from “bias” generally to **harmful bias**, and embeds that within a broader fairness analysis. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.7; NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.3.*

### 6. Privacy became “Privacy-Enhanced”

Draft 1 used **“Privacy”** as a socio-technical characteristic. *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.2.3.* Draft 2 and AI RMF 1.0 use **“Privacy-Enhanced.”** *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.7; NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.6.*

AI RMF 1.0 frames privacy as norms and practices that safeguard autonomy, identity, and dignity, and it specifically points to privacy-enhancing technologies and data-minimizing methods such as de-identification and aggregation. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.6.* The substantive shift is from privacy as an abstract value to privacy as a design and risk-management objective. *NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.6.*

### Bottom line

Compared with the 2022 working drafts, **NIST AI RMF 1.0 mainly makes the trustworthiness characteristics more integrated, operational, and governance-oriented**. Draft 1 separated technical characteristics, socio-technical characteristics, and guiding principles. Draft 2 moved closer to the final structure. The January 2023 final version crystallized the model into seven characteristics, clarified that **validity and reliability are foundational**, made **accountability and transparency cross-cutting**, distinguished **security from resilience**, reframed fairness as **harmful-bias management plus broader equity concerns**, and recast privacy as **privacy-enhanced AI**. *NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 1, §5.1–§5.3; NIST AI RMF 2022 Draft 2, §4.1–§4.7; NIST AI RMF 1.0, §3.1–§3.7 and Fig. 4.*

question.question: What changed between the 2021 Commission proposal for the EU AI Act and the final 2024 text in terms of obligations on general-purpose AI / foundation models?
question.expected_answer: The 2021 proposal did not address general-purpose AI; the final 2024 text added a dedicated chapter (Title VIIIa) on general-purpose AI models with two tiers of obligations: (1) baseline obligations for all GPAI providers — technical documentation, instructions for downstream providers, copyright policy, summary of training data; (2) additional obligations for 'GPAI with systemic risk' (designated by compute threshold or Commission decision) — model evaluations including adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, serious-incident reporting, cybersecurity, and energy reporting.

output.answer:
## Short answer

The 2021 Commission proposal had **no dedicated regime for “general-purpose AI” or “foundation models.”** It regulated **AI systems** mainly through prohibited uses, high-risk AI-system obligations, and a few transparency duties. The final 2024 EU AI Act adds an entirely new **Chapter V on general-purpose AI (GPAI) models**, creating direct obligations for model providers even before a model is integrated into a downstream AI system.  
Key new obligations include **model technical documentation, downstream-provider information, copyright compliance policies, public training-data-content summaries, EU authorised representatives for non-EU providers, systemic-risk evaluations/mitigations, incident reporting, cybersecurity, codes of practice, and Commission enforcement/fines**.  

## Main changes

| Topic | 2021 Commission proposal | Final 2024 EU AI Act |
|---|---|---|
| Dedicated “foundation model” / GPAI category | **Absent.** The proposal regulated “AI systems” and operators such as providers, users, importers, distributors; it did not define or regulate “general-purpose AI model” or “foundation model” as a separate object. The high-risk regime turned on whether an **AI system** met Article 6 / Annex III criteria. | **Added.** The final Act defines a **“general-purpose AI model”** as a model trained with large amounts of data, showing significant generality, able to perform a wide range of tasks, and integrable into downstream systems, excluding pre-market R&D/prototyping models. It also defines “general-purpose AI system,” “downstream provider,” “high-impact capabilities,” and “systemic risk.” **EU AI Act 2024, Article 3(63)–(66).** |
| Trigger for obligations | Obligations generally attached to **high-risk AI systems** or certain transparency-triggering AI systems. High-risk classification depended on safety-component/product rules or Annex III use cases. **2021 proposal, Article 6.** | Obligations attach directly to **providers placing GPAI models on the Union market**, irrespective of a specific downstream use case. The final Act expressly lays down “harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models.” **EU AI Act 2024, Article 1(2)(e), Article 2(1)(a), Chapter V.** |
| Baseline documentation for model providers | No model-level technical-documentation duty for foundation/GPAI models as such. Documentation duties existed for high-risk AI systems, e.g., information enabling users to interpret outputs and use systems appropriately. **2021 proposal, Article 13; Article 6.** | GPAI model providers must draw up and keep up-to-date **technical documentation of the model**, including training/testing processes and evaluation results, for the AI Office and competent authorities. **EU AI Act 2024, Article 53(1)(a), Annex XI.** |
| Information to downstream providers | No dedicated obligation for a general-purpose model provider to support downstream AI-system providers. Duties were framed around high-risk AI-system providers giving instructions and information to users. **2021 proposal, Article 13.** | GPAI model providers must make available information and documentation to downstream AI-system providers so they can understand the model’s capabilities/limitations and comply with their own AI Act obligations. **EU AI Act 2024, Article 53(1)(b), Annex XII.** |
| Copyright and training data transparency | No GPAI-specific copyright-policy or training-data-summary obligation. | GPAI model providers must put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law, including reservations of rights under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790, and must publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content using an AI Office template. **EU AI Act 2024, Article 53(1)(c)–(d).** |
| Open-source treatment | No specific open-source GPAI carve-out, because no GPAI regime existed. | Providers of free/open-source GPAI models are exempt from the Article 53(1)(a) and (b) documentation/downstream-information duties if weights, architecture and usage information are public, but the exemption does **not** apply to GPAI models with systemic risk. **EU AI Act 2024, Article 53(2).** |
| Systemic-risk tier | No systemic-risk tier for foundation models. High-risk obligations were use-case/product based. **2021 proposal, Article 6 and Annex III.** | Final text creates **GPAI models with systemic risk**, including models with high-impact capabilities or those designated by the Commission using Annex XIII criteria. **EU AI Act 2024, Article 51; Annex XIII.** |
| Extra duties for most powerful models | Not applicable. | Providers of GPAI models with systemic risk must perform model evaluations, including adversarial testing where appropriate; assess and mitigate systemic risks; track, document and report serious incidents and corrective measures; and ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity. **EU AI Act 2024, Article 55(1).** |

| Enforcement | Enforcement in the proposal focused on AI systems/operators, especially high-risk systems and transparency obligations. | The Commission can fine GPAI model providers up to **EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover**, whichever is higher, for intentional or negligent infringements, failure to provide information, failure to comply with measures, or failure to provide model access for evaluation. **EU AI Act 2024, Article 101(1).** |

## Practical compliance significance

1. **The regulatory object changed from “AI system” only to “AI system + AI model.”**  
   In 2021, a foundation-model developer might avoid direct AI Act duties unless its offering was itself a covered AI system or was placed into a high-risk or transparency-triggering use. Under the final Act, placing a GPAI model on the EU market directly triggers obligations. **2021 proposal, Article 6; EU AI Act 2024, Articles 1(2)(e), 2(1)(a), 3(63), 53.**

2. **The final Act creates upstream supply-chain accountability.**  
   GPAI model providers must give downstream AI-system providers enough information to understand capabilities and limitations and to comply with the Act. This is a major change from the 2021 proposal’s focus on high-risk system providers giving instructions to users. **2021 proposal, Article 13; EU AI Act 2024, Article 53(1)(b), Annex XII.**

3. **Training data and copyright became explicit compliance topics.**  
   The final Act adds a copyright-compliance policy and a public training-content summary for GPAI models. These were not present as GPAI-specific obligations in the 2021 proposal. **EU AI Act 2024, Article 53(1)(c)–(d).**

4. **The final Act adds a two-tier GPAI regime.**  
   All GPAI model providers have baseline Article 53 obligations; providers of GPAI models with systemic risk have additional Article 55 duties, including evaluations, systemic-risk assessment/mitigation, incident reporting, and cybersecurity. **EU AI Act 2024, Articles 51, 53, 55.**

5. **Open-source models get limited relief, but not if systemic-risk.**  
   The final text exempts certain open-source GPAI models from some documentation and downstream-information obligations, but not copyright/training-summary obligations and not where the model has systemic risk. **EU AI Act 2024, Article 53(2).**

6. **Governance shifted toward central EU oversight.**  
   GPAI obligations are supervised through the Commission/AI Office architecture, codes of practice, and specific fines for GPAI model providers. **EU AI Act 2024, Articles 53(3)–(4), 56, 101.**

### Article 9: Risk Management System

1. A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems.

2. The risk management system shall be understood as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating. It shall comprise the following steps:

(a) the identification and analysis of the known and the reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose;

(b) the estimation and evaluation of the risks that may emerge when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose, and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse;

(c) the evaluation of other risks possibly arising, based on the analysis of data gathered from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72;

(d) the adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures designed to address the risks identified pursuant to point (a).

3. The risks referred to in this Article shall concern only those which may be reasonably mitigated or eliminated through the development or design of the high-risk AI system, or the provision of adequate technical information.

### Article 27: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems

1. Prior to deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), with the exception of high-risk AI systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III, shall perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights that the use of such system may produce. (a) a description of the deployer's processes in which the high-risk AI system will be used in line with its intended purpose;

(b) a description of the period of time within which, and the frequency with which, each high-risk AI system is intended to be used;

(c) the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected by its use in the specific context;

(d) the specific risks of harm likely to have an impact on the categories of natural persons or groups of persons identified pursuant to point (c) of this paragraph, taking into account the information given by the provider pursuant to Article 13;

(e) a description of the implementation of human oversight measures, according to the instructions for use;

# Chapter I: General Provisions (Articles 1-4)

## Article 1: Subject Matter

1. The purpose of this Regulation is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union and supporting innovation.

2. This Regulation lays down:

(a) harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems in the Union;

(b) prohibitions of certain AI practices;

(c) specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems;

(d) harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems;

(e) harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models;

(f) rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement;

(g) measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including startups.

## Article 2: Scope

1. This Regulation applies to:

(a) providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems or placing on the market general-purpose AI models in the Union, irrespective of whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country;

(b) deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located within the Union;

(c) providers and deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located in a third country, where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union;

(d) importers and distributors of AI systems;

(e) product manufacturers placing on the market or putting into service an AI system together with their product and under their own name or trademark;

(f) authorised representatives of providers, which are not established in the Union;

(g) affected persons that are located in the Union.

**Article 15: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity**
### Article 15: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity

1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.

2. To address the technical aspects of how to measure the appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness set out in paragraph 1 and any other relevant performance metrics, the Commission shall, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders and organisations such as metrology and benchmarking authorities, encourage, as appropriate, the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies.

3. The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use.

4. High-risk AI systems shall be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates, in particular due to their interaction with natural persons or other systems. Technical and organisational measures shall be taken in this regard.

The robustness of high-risk AI systems may be achieved through technical redundancy solutions, which may include backup or fail-safe plans.

High-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service shall be developed in such a way as to eliminate or reduce as far as possible the risk of possibly biased outputs influencing input for future operations (feedback loops), and as to ensure that any such feedback loops are duly addressed with appropriate mitigation measures.

5. High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities. The technical solutions aiming to ensure the cybersecurity of high-risk AI systems shall be appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks.

The technical solutions to address AI specific vulnerabilities shall include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks trying to manipulate the training data set (data poisoning), or pre-trained components used in training (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the AI model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks or model flaws.

(e) technical specifications, including standards, to be applied and, where the relevant harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all of the relevant requirements set out in Section 2, the means to be used to ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with those requirements;

(h) the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system, in accordance with Article 72;

(i) procedures related to the reporting of a serious incident in accordance with Article 73;

(k) systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information;

**Article 26: Obligations of Deployers of High-Risk AI Systems**
### Article 26: Obligations of Deployers of High-Risk AI Systems

1. Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use such systems in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying the systems, pursuant to paragraphs 3 and 6.

2. Deployers shall assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support.

3. The obligations set out in paragraphs 1 and 2, are without prejudice to other deployer obligations under Union or national law and to the deployer's freedom to organise its own resources and activities for the purpose of implementing the human oversight measures indicated by the provider.

4. Without prejudice to paragraphs 1 and 2, to the extent the deployer exercises control over the input data, that deployer shall ensure that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.

5. Deployers shall monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use and, where relevant, inform providers in accordance with Article 72. Where deployers have reason to consider that the use of the high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions may result in that AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), they shall, without undue delay, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and shall suspend the use of that system. Where deployers have identified a serious incident, they shall also immediately inform first the provider, and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities of that incident. If the deployer is not able to reach the provider, Article 73 shall apply mutatis mutandis.

This obligation shall not cover sensitive operational data of deployers of AI systems which are law enforcement authorities.

For deployers that are financial institutions subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law, the monitoring obligation set out in the first subparagraph shall be deemed to be fulfilled by complying with the rules on internal governance arrangements, processes and mechanisms pursuant to the relevant financial service law.

6. Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs automatically generated by that high-risk AI system to the extent such logs are under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data.

### Article 22: Authorised Representatives of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems

1. Prior to making their high-risk AI systems available on the Union market, providers established in third countries shall, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative which is established in the Union.

2. The provider shall enable its authorised representative to perform the tasks specified in the mandate received from the provider.

3. The authorised representative shall perform the tasks specified in the mandate received from the provider. It shall provide a copy of the mandate to the market surveillance authorities upon request, in one of the official languages of the institutions of the Union, as indicated by the competent authority. For the purposes of this Regulation, the mandate shall empower the authorised representative to carry out the following tasks:

(a) verify that the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and the technical documentation referred to in Article 11 have been drawn up and that an appropriate conformity assessment procedure has been carried out by the provider;

(b) keep at the disposal of the competent authorities and national authorities or bodies referred to in Article 74(10), for a period of 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service, the contact details of the provider that appointed the authorised representative, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47, the technical documentation and, if applicable, the certificate issued by the notified body;

(c) provide a competent authority, upon a reasoned request, with all the information and documentation, including that referred to in point (b) of this subparagraph, necessary to demonstrate the conformity of a high-risk AI system with the requirements set out in Section 2, including access to the logs, as referred to in Article 12(1), automatically generated by the high-risk AI system, to the extent such logs are under the control of the provider;

(d) cooperate with competent authorities, upon a reasoned request, in any action the latter take in relation to the high-risk AI system, in particular to reduce and mitigate the risks posed by the high-risk AI system;

(e) where applicable, comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49(1), or, if the registration is carried out by the provider itself, ensure that the information referred to in point 3 of Section A of Annex VIII is correct.

The mandate shall empower the authorised representative to be addressed, in addition to or instead of the provider, by the competent authorities, on all issues related to ensuring compliance with this Regulation.

**Article 21: Cooperation with Competent Authorities**
### Article 21: Cooperation with Competent Authorities

1. Providers of high-risk AI systems shall, upon a reasoned request by a competent authority, provide that authority all the information and documentation necessary to demonstrate the conformity of the high-risk AI system with the requirements set out in Section 2, in a language which can be easily understood by the authority in one of the official languages of the institutions of the Union as indicated by the Member State concerned.

2. Upon a reasoned request by a competent authority, providers shall also give the requesting competent authority, as applicable, access to the automatically generated logs of the high-risk AI system referred to in Article 12(1), to the extent such logs are under their control.

3. Any information obtained by a competent authority pursuant to this Article shall be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations set out in Article 78.

question.question: What are the most significant differences between the 1995 EU Data Protection Directive (95/46/EC) and the 2018 GDPR for organisations processing personal data?
question.expected_answer: Key differences: (1) Regulation vs Directive — GDPR is directly applicable across the EU, not requiring national transposition; (2) extraterritorial scope — GDPR applies to non-EU controllers offering goods/services to or monitoring EU data subjects; (3) explicit accountability — Articles 5(2), 24, 30 require demonstrable compliance and records of processing; (4) DPO obligation for certain entities (Article 37); (5) DPIA requirement (Article 35); (6) breach notification (Articles 33-34); (7) much higher fines (up to 4% of global turnover or €20M); (8) new/expanded data-subject rights (erasure, portability, automated-decision objection); (9) explicit data-protection-by-design (Article 25).

output.answer:
Below are the most significant practical differences for organisations processing personal data.

| Area | 1995 Data Protection Directive 95/46/EC | GDPR, applicable from 2018 | Why it matters for organisations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legal form and harmonisation | The 1995 regime was a **Directive**, so Member States had to transpose it into national law, creating variation across the EU. It was repealed by the GDPR. **Directive 95/46/EC; GDPR Art. 94** | The GDPR is an EU **Regulation**, designed to apply as a single directly applicable framework across the EU from 25 May 2018. **GDPR Arts. 94, 99** | Multinational organisations moved from managing many national implementations to a more unified EU-wide compliance programme, although Member State derogations still exist in areas such as employment, public interest and special-category processing. **GDPR Art. 6(2)–(3), Ch. IX** |
| Territorial reach | The Directive focused mainly on processing in the context of an EU establishment, with more limited rules for non-EU controllers using equipment in the EU. **Directive 95/46/EC Art. 4** | The GDPR expressly applies to non-EU controllers and processors that offer goods or services to individuals in the EU or monitor their behaviour in the EU. **GDPR Art. 3(2)** | Many non-EU businesses with EU users, customers, tracking, analytics or behavioural advertising came within scope. Such organisations may also need an EU representative. **GDPR Arts. 3, 27** |
| Accountability and evidence of compliance | The Directive contained core data protection principles, security duties and notification requirements, but it was less explicit about an organisation-wide duty to prove compliance. **Directive 95/46/EC Arts. 6, 17–20** | The GDPR makes accountability explicit: controllers must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures and be able to demonstrate compliance. **GDPR Art. 24; see also Art. 5(2)** | Compliance became more documentation-heavy: policies, records, risk assessments, governance evidence and auditability are central. **GDPR Arts. 24, 30, 35** |
| Prior notification vs risk-based governance | The Directive generally required controllers to notify supervisory authorities before processing, with possible prior checks for risky processing. **Directive 95/46/EC Arts. 18–20** | The GDPR largely replaces broad prior notification with risk-based obligations such as records of processing, data protection impact assessments and prior consultation only where high residual risk remains. **GDPR Arts. 30, 35, 36** | Organisations shifted from registration-style compliance to ongoing risk management and documented internal controls. |
| Data protection by design and default | The Directive required security and compliance with principles such as purpose limitation, data quality and proportionality, but did not contain the GDPR’s express “by design and by default” obligation. **Directive 95/46/EC Arts. 6, 17** | Controllers must implement data protection by design and by default, including measures such as pseudonymisation and ensuring that, by default, only necessary personal data are processed. **GDPR Art. 25** | Privacy requirements must be built into product, system and process design, not added only after launch. |
| Processor obligations | Under the Directive, processors were addressed mainly through controller obligations and contracts requiring processing only on instructions and appropriate security. **Directive 95/46/EC Art. 17** | The GDPR imposes direct statutory obligations on processors, including security, sub-processor controls, assistance to controllers, deletion/return of data, audit support and processing only on documented instructions. **GDPR Arts. 28, 29, 32** | Vendors, cloud providers, SaaS providers and other processors became directly accountable and exposed to regulatory enforcement and liability. **GDPR Arts. 28, 82, 83** |
| Data subject rights | The Directive provided rights such as access, rectification, erasure/blocking, objection and protections against certain automated decisions. **Directive 95/46/EC Arts. 12, 14, 15** | The GDPR strengthens and expands rights, including more detailed access rights, erasure/right to be forgotten, restriction, portability, objection and rights related to automated decision-making and profiling. **GDPR Arts. 15, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22** | Organisations need formal request-handling workflows, identity verification, response tracking, deletion processes and portability capabilities where applicable. |
| Transparency requirements | The Directive required controllers to provide information about identity, purposes, recipients and rights when data were collected or obtained. **Directive 95/46/EC Arts. 10–11** | The GDPR requires more detailed notices, including legal basis, legitimate interests, retention periods, DPO contact details, transfer safeguards, complaint rights, portability, withdrawal of consent and automated decision-making information. **GDPR Arts. 13–14** | Privacy notices became longer, more structured and more operationally tied to actual processing records. |
| Consent standard | The Directive recognised consent as a lawful basis and defined it as freely given, specific and informed. **Directive 95/46/EC Arts. 2(h), 7(a)** | The GDPR requires consent to be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, given by statement or clear affirmative action; it also adds detailed conditions for demonstrating consent and withdrawal. **GDPR Arts. 4(11), 6(1)(a), 7** | Pre-ticked boxes, implied consent and poorly evidenced consent became much harder to rely on. |
| Breach notification | The Directive did not contain a general EU-wide personal data breach notification duty for all controllers; breach notification was mostly sector-specific under other EU laws. **Directive 95/46/EC Art. 17** | Controllers must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours unless the breach is unlikely to pose risk; processors must notify controllers without undue delay. High-risk breaches must also be communicated to affected individuals. **GDPR Arts. 33–34** | Incident response, breach assessment, logging and escalation processes became mandatory operational controls. |
| Data Protection Officers | The Directive allowed Member States to provide notification exemptions where a data protection official was appointed, but it did not create the GDPR’s harmonised DPO regime. **Directive 95/46/EC Art. 18(2)** | The GDPR requires DPOs in specific cases, including certain public authorities, large-scale systematic monitoring and large-scale processing of special categories or criminal-offence data; it also defines DPO tasks. **GDPR Arts. 37–39** | Many organisations had to appoint independent, expert privacy officers with monitoring, advisory, training and supervisory-authority liaison functions. |
| International transfers | The Directive restricted transfers to third countries without adequate protection, using adequacy findings, safeguards or derogations. **Directive 95/46/EC Arts. 25–26** | The GDPR keeps the transfer architecture but elaborates it: adequacy decisions, appropriate safeguards, binding corporate rules, standard clauses, codes/certifications and derogations, with an overarching rule that GDPR protection must not be undermined. **GDPR Arts. 44–49** | Cross-border transfer governance became more detailed, especially for global cloud, outsourcing and group-company transfers. |
| Enforcement and sanctions | The Directive required Member States to provide sanctions and remedies, but penalty levels varied significantly by country. **Directive 95/46/EC Arts. 22–24** | The GDPR creates EU-wide administrative fine tiers: up to €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover for the most serious infringements, whichever is higher. **GDPR Art. 83** | Regulatory risk became much more material at board level. |
| Supervisory authority cooperation | The Directive required independent supervisory authorities but enforcement remained more nationally fragmented. **Directive 95/46/EC Art. 28** | The GDPR introduces cooperation and consistency mechanisms and a lead supervisory authority concept for cross-border processing. **GDPR Arts. 56, 60, 63, 68** | Organisations operating across Member States can often deal primarily with a lead authority, but cross-border cases can involve coordinated EU-level enforcement. |
| Remedies and liability | The Directive provided judicial remedies, liability and sanctions through Member State implementation. **Directive 95/46/EC Arts. 22–24** | The GDPR gives data subjects complaint rights, judicial remedies and compensation rights, and expressly addresses controller and processor liability. **GDPR Arts. 77, 79, 82** | Litigation and compensation exposure increased, including for processors in certain circumstances. |

**Bottom line:** the GDPR did not replace the Directive’s core principles—lawfulness, fairness, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security and individual rights remain recognisable from the 1995 framework. The major change is that GDPR turns those principles into a more prescriptive, risk-based, documented and enforceable compliance regime, with broader territorial scope, direct processor obligations, stronger individual rights, mandatory breach notification, data protection by design/default, DPIAs, DPO requirements in specified cases, and much higher penalties.

question.question: Did the 2022 update to the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria (the 'Points of Focus' update) change the certifiable criteria themselves, or only the guidance? Summarise.
question.expected_answer: The 2022 update primarily revised the 'points of focus' that accompany the criteria — i.e., the implementation guidance — without changing the criteria language itself for the most part. Material refinements were aimed at supply-chain risk, considering risks from environmental and emerging threats, communication of confidentiality commitments, and clearer treatment of system change management. Auditors continue to opine against the criteria; the points of focus inform how controls are evaluated.

output.answer:
No. The 2022 SOC 2 update did **not** change the certifiable Trust Services Criteria themselves; it revised the **Points of Focus** associated with certain criteria.

Summary:

- The document remains the **“2017 Trust Services Criteria for Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy”**, now labeled **“with Revised Points of Focus — 2022.”** The title itself indicates the base criteria remain the 2017 TSC, with 2022 revisions to points of focus. **SOC 2, TSP Section 100, Notice to Readers / Revisions in This Version.**

- The 2022 version says it was “modified to reflect **new points of focus and edits to extant points of focus**” relevant to certain Trust Services Criteria. It does not say the criteria were replaced or amended. **SOC 2, TSP Section 100, Revisions in This Version.**

- Points of Focus are described as representing “important characteristics of the criteria” and as assisting management and practitioners in evaluating whether controls are suitably designed and operating effectively. That makes them supporting guidance/considerations, not the certifiable criteria themselves. **SOC 2, TSP Section 100, Revisions in This Version.**

- In a SOC 2 examination, the service auditor’s opinion is on whether controls are suitably designed and, for Type 2, operating effectively to achieve the service organization’s commitments and requirements **based on the applicable Trust Services Criteria**. **SOC 2, Description Criteria, ¶.03 and SOC 2, TSP Section 100, ¶.13.**

- For each Trust Services category in scope, completeness is determined by addressing the applicable **criteria** for that category, not by treating every Point of Focus as a standalone certifiable requirement. **SOC 2, TSP Section 100, ¶.10–.11.**

Bottom line: the 2022 update changed the **Points of Focus**—the explanatory/interpretive characteristics used to help apply the criteria—but not the underlying SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria that form the basis of the audit opinion.

question.question: How has SR 11-7 guidance on ongoing model monitoring evolved between the 2011 original and the 2026 SR 26-2 revision, particularly for AI/ML models?
question.expected_answer: The 2011 SR 11-7 emphasised periodic outcomes analysis and back-testing for static statistical models, with monitoring frequency tied to model risk-tier. SR 26-2 (2026) explicitly extends monitoring to AI/ML: continuous monitoring of distributional drift, performance decay, fairness/bias metrics, and emergent behaviour; explicit treatment of self-learning systems with retraining controls; vendor-AI-model monitoring obligations; and tighter governance over model changes via continuous-deployment pipelines. The 2026 revision treats the model lifecycle as continuous rather than periodic.

output.answer:
SR 11-7’s monitoring guidance has evolved from a relatively **periodic validation-control concept** in 2011 into a more **lifecycle, risk-based performance management concept** in the 2026 SR 26-2 revision—especially relevant for AI/ML models that can drift, be frequently updated, depend on changing data, or be supplied by vendors.

| Topic | 2011 SR 11-7 original | 2026 SR 26-2 revision / revised SR 11-7 | Practical implication for AI/ML |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Role of monitoring** | Ongoing monitoring was one of the core elements of model validation, alongside conceptual soundness and outcomes analysis. It focused on whether the model continued to operate as intended and whether changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, or market conditions required adjustment, redevelopment, or replacement. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § III “Model Validation,” including “Ongoing Monitoring.” | Monitoring is framed more explicitly as part of **“Model Validation and Monitoring”** and is defined as evaluating whether a model is performing as expected given changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, **data relevance**, or market conditions. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § V “Model Validation and Monitoring,” “Ongoing Model Monitoring.” | AI/ML monitoring should not be limited to periodic validation reports; it should continuously or regularly evaluate performance against changing data, population, business use, and environment. |
| **Triggers for action** | The 2011 guidance emphasized that monitoring should identify when model changes, replacement, or redevelopment may be needed because conditions have changed. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § III “Model Validation,” “Ongoing Monitoring.” | The 2026 revision is more explicit that a model that no longer performs as expected may warrant **overlays, adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment**, depending on the organization’s model risk management policy for model deterioration. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § V “Model Validation and Monitoring,” “Ongoing Model Monitoring.” | For AI/ML, monitoring programs should define drift thresholds and escalation actions—e.g., human overlays, feature/input controls, recalibration, retraining, or full redevelopment. |
| **Data relevance and drift** | The 2011 guidance addressed changes in business and market conditions, and expected monitoring to assess whether the model remained appropriate. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § III “Model Validation,” “Ongoing Monitoring.” | The 2026 revision expressly includes **data relevance** as a monitoring consideration. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § V “Model Validation and Monitoring,” “Ongoing Model Monitoring.” | This is a major AI/ML-relevant evolution: monitoring should include input data drift, feature distribution shifts, population stability, label/outcome changes, and data quality deterioration. |
| **Performance thresholds** | The 2011 framework used outcomes analysis, back-testing, and benchmarking to identify model performance issues. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § III “Model Validation,” “Outcomes Analysis” and “Ongoing Monitoring.” | The 2026 revision states that outcomes analysis and validation may identify **material errors or persistent deviations outside established performance thresholds**, which may require adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § V “Model Validation and Monitoring,” “Outcomes Analysis.” | AI/ML monitoring should define measurable performance thresholds, not only qualitative review—for example accuracy, calibration, false positive/false negative rates, stability, fairness-related metrics where relevant, and business outcome metrics. |
| **Model limitations** | The 2011 guidance expected organizations to understand model limitations and evaluate whether models remained appropriate for their intended use. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § III “Model Validation” and § II “Model Development, Implementation, and Use.” | The 2026 revision states that an effective monitoring plan may include regularly assessing model limitations identified during development **and over time**, with procedures for responding to issues before and after approval for use. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § V “Model Validation and Monitoring,” “Ongoing Model Monitoring.” | For AI/ML, limitations should be treated as living risk items—e.g., explainability limits, training-data representativeness, out-of-distribution behavior, instability after retraining, and limitations in human interpretability. |
| **Frequency and tailoring** | The 2011 guidance required ongoing monitoring at regular intervals appropriate to the model’s risk and use. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § III “Model Validation,” “Ongoing Monitoring.” | The 2026 revision emphasizes that validation timing, nature, and frequency vary based on model purpose, methodology, frequency and scope of model changes, data limitations, and other constraints. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § V “Model Validation and Monitoring.” | AI/ML models that are frequently retrained, use dynamic data, or materially affect decisions should be monitored more frequently and with greater automation than stable, low-impact models. |
| **Monitoring before full validation is complete** | The 2011 guidance generally expected validation before use, with controls around implementation and use. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § III “Model Validation.” | The 2026 revision expressly recognizes that urgent business needs may lead to model use before validation is complete, but requires heightened attention to limitations, communication to stakeholders, appropriate controls, limits on use, or closer performance monitoring. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § V “Model Validation and Monitoring.” | For AI/ML pilots or rapid deployments, banks should document limited-use conditions, compensating controls, user notices, enhanced monitoring, and exit criteria. |
| **Interpretability and benchmarking** | The 2011 guidance included benchmarking and outcomes analysis as validation tools. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § III “Model Validation,” “Benchmarking” and “Outcomes Analysis.” | The 2026 revision expressly notes that, for some models, **interpretability measures or benchmarking to other models** may be more practical than purely theoretical evaluation. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § V “Model Validation and Monitoring,” “Conceptual Soundness.” | This is particularly relevant to complex AI/ML models where source-code or mathematical transparency may be limited; banks may need explainability techniques, challenger models, sensitivity testing, and benchmark comparisons. |
| **Effective challenge across lifecycle** | The 2011 guidance required effective challenge as a core model risk management principle. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § I–III, model risk management and validation principles. | The 2026 revision states that effective challenge applies throughout the model lifecycle, from model development to ongoing monitoring, and must be performed by objective experts with appropriate expertise, independence, standing, and influence. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § III “Model Risk Management.” | AI/ML monitoring should involve personnel with ML, data science, domain, risk, and control expertise—not just business owners or developers. |
| **Aggregate and common-dependency risk** | The 2011 guidance recognized model risk across models and required inventory and governance. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § IV “Governance, Policies, and Controls.” | The 2026 revision highlights aggregate model risk, including interactions and dependencies among models and reliance on common assumptions, data, or methodologies. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § III “Model Risk Management.” | AI/ML portfolios often share data pipelines, embeddings, vendor platforms, feature stores, or foundation models; monitoring should detect correlated failures, not just single-model performance issues. |
| **Vendor / third-party models** | The 2011 guidance required validation of vendor models even when proprietary information was limited. **Citation:** SR 11-7, 2011, § VII “Vendor and Other Third-Party Products.” | The 2026 revision states that organizations should understand vendor model conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance, and should conduct ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis to assess whether vendor models remain accurate, fit for purpose, and reliable. **Citation:** SR 26-2 / revised SR 11-7, § VII “Vendor and Other Third-Party Products.” | For AI/ML vendor tools, banks cannot rely solely on vendor attestations; they need production monitoring, performance testing on bank data, change controls, and evidence that the tool remains fit for the bank’s use case. |

**Bottom line:** the 2011 SR 11-7 guidance treated ongoing monitoring as a core validation activity to ensure a model remained appropriate as conditions changed. The 2026 SR 26-2 revision keeps that foundation but modernizes it by emphasizing **risk-based tailoring, data relevance, model deterioration, thresholds, overlays, recalibration, redevelopment, lifecycle limitations, interpretability, vendor-model monitoring, and aggregate dependencies**. For AI/ML models, that means monitoring must cover not only output accuracy but also **data drift, model drift, retraining effects, changing use cases, explainability limits, vendor changes, and portfolio-level dependencies**.

Outcomes analysis compares model outputs to corresponding real-world outcomes to

other elements of the validation process may identify material errors or persistent deviations

Outcomes analysis can take many forms, including testing conducted during model 
development, reports or analysis performed as part of ongoing monitoring, or standalone 
activities such as back-testing or outlier analysis. A banking organization’s approach depends on 
the model’s objectives, methodology, and data availability. As part of model validation, sound 
practice involves reviewing outcomes analysis to evaluate the reasonableness and 
appropriateness of the results, with additional analysis and testing, if warranted. When a model’s 
design relies substantially on expert judgment, quantitative outcomes analysis helps to evaluate 
the quality of that judgment.  
Ongoing Model Monitoring 
Ongoing model monitoring involves an evaluation of the extent to which a model is 
performing as expected given potential changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data 
relevance, or market conditions. A model that no longer performs as expected may warrant 
overlays, adjustment, or redevelopment of the model depending on a banking organization’s 
model risk management policy as it pertains to model deterioration.  
An effective ongoing monitoring plan may also include regularly assessing any model 
limitations at the development stage and over time, along with procedures for responding to any 
issues that may occur, before and after a model is approved for use. The frequency and scope of

business insights that enhance future development. Constructive engagement, particularly around 
model design, assumptions, and outcomes, strengthens both model understanding and model 
quality. Using a model beyond its intended purpose introduces additional uncertainty and risk. 
When extending a model’s use beyond its original application, sound practice involves 
considering additional analysis of the new usage and its limitations, along with review of 
existing controls to manage the resulting risk.

Model validation evaluates whether models perform as expected and includes an 
assessment of a model’s reliability and its limitations. The nature and rigor of validation generally 
align with the model’s approach, use, and materiality. Sound validation identifies model 
limitations and errors and clarifies appropriate use and whether corrective actions may be

Validation provides insight into the reliability of a given model, based on its underlying

characterize the source and extent of the model risk. Validation can reveal performance 
deterioration over time and inform judgments about acceptable performance ranges. When 
performance deviates meaningfully from expectations, banking organizations generally consider 
whether model adjustments, recalibration, or redevelopment are warranted.  
The timing, nature, and frequency of validation activities vary based on model purpose, 
model methodology, frequency and scope of model changes, data limitations, and other practical 
constraints. Sound practice recognizes that validation approaches may differ across models based 
on their characteristics and use. Validation generally occurs prior to a model’s first use.

8  
However, certain circumstances (e.g., an urgent business need) may necessitate using the model 
before validation is completed. In those cases, sound practice involves greater attention to the 
model’s limitations when considering the appropriateness of its use, informing relevant 
stakeholders of those limitations, and determining appropriate controls (e.g., placing limits on 
model use or more closely monitoring its performance).  
The quality of validation process depends on the rigor and effectiveness of the review 
rather than on organizational structure of the banking organization’s risk management function. 
Technical knowledge and modeling expertise enable appropriate analysis, meaningful critique, 
and sound judgment about model performance and risk.   
Even with sound modeling practices and rigorous validation, material model risk can 
remain. Users of model output benefit from understanding and communicating limitations, 
monitoring performance, periodically reviewing relevance, and supplementing model output 
with complementary analysis and information. 
Components of Model Validation 
Conceptual Soundness 
Validating conceptual soundness involves assessing and documenting model design 
(including key modeling choices, assumptions, qualitative judgments, and data selection), 
construction, and developmental testing. While evaluating theoretical construction may be 
important for some models, other assessments—such as interpretability measures or 
benchmarking to other models—may be more practical for other models. Sound practice subjects 
modeling aspects to critical analysis by evaluating both the quality and extent of developmental 
evidence. 
Outcomes Analysis

5  
Sound practice involves assessing model risk both individually and in aggregate. 
Aggregate risk reflects interactions and dependencies among models; reliance on common 
assumptions, data, or methodologies; and any other factors that could adversely affect several 
models and their outputs simultaneously.   
Sound model risk management also involves “effective challenge,” which refers to the 
critical analysis conducted by objective experts who evaluate model risk and effect appropriate 
changes throughout the model lifecycle, from model development to ongoing monitoring. 
Effective challenge is performed by individuals with the appropriate expertise to conduct a 
critical and objective challenge, sufficient independence to maintain objectivity, as well as the 
organizational standing and influence to effect any change. 
The size and complexity of the banking organization’s operations also may influence the 
range of model risk management. A banking organization with simple operations may not 
conduct model risk management with the same rigor as an organization with relatively more 
complex operations. Furthermore, a banking organization may tailor portions of its model risk 
management practices that are relevant to the risks posed by a particular model and with a level 
of rigor commensurate with that risk. Effective model risk management therefore warrants 
consideration of model risk in the context of the broader business risks that models support or 
influence. 
IV. MODEL DEVELOPMENT AND MODEL USE 
Model Development 
Sound model development activities are aligned with model purpose, business use, and 
banking organization policy. Model development is not purely a technical exercise. The 
developer’s judgment influences the model’s conceptual design and soundness, inputs,

6  
assumptions, and methodology, all of which affect a model’s inherent risk. Because model 
development is often multidisciplinary, tailored to actual use, and involves significant 
subjectivity throughout its lifecycle, sound development practices are important for effective 
model risk management.  
An effective development process generally begins with a clear statement of purpose to 
maximize the likelihood that model development is aligned with the intended use. This 
fundamental step supports decision-making throughout the development lifecycle, including the 
selection of data, methodologies, and testing approaches. 
Input from model users can enhance model development by providing business context 
and practical insights. Business managers affected by model outcomes may raise questions about 
the methods or assumptions, particularly when the outcomes are unexpected. Constructive 
engagement around model design and assumptions strengthens both model understanding and 
model quality. 
Model testing is a core component of model development that evaluates whether a model 
performs as intended. Testing may include a range of activities, from out-of-sample and out-of-
time testing, to a comparison of alternative assumptions and methodologies, to a critical 
assessment of data quality, relevance, and inputs. Testing may be performed by model 
developers in collaboration with model users. The specific approach depends on the model’s 
characteristics. The rigor of effective testing is commensurate with model complexity and 
materiality. For models that have relatively less material impact or for banking organizations 
with relatively less complex operations, model testing may be more limited in scope.  
Model Use 
Effective model use depends on a clear understanding of a model’s limitations. Model

11  
broader model risk management activities. Organizations benefit from clearly defining roles and 
responsibilities when delegating these activities.  
Model Inventory 
It is common industry practice for banking organizations to maintain a comprehensive set 
of information for models under development or in use to support effective model risk 
management. While the inventory may contain varying levels of information to reflect different 
levels of model complexity and a banking organization’s overall level of model usage, an 
effective model inventory includes sufficient information to understand model risks, so as to 
support effective model risk management at the individual and aggregate levels.  
Documentation 
Adequate documentation helps to support effective model risk management. For 
example, documentation can help maximize the likelihood of continuity of operations, including 
supporting the tracking of recommendations, responses, and exceptions; it can also be used to 
more effectively help manage any model remediation efforts.   
VII. VENDOR AND OTHER THIRD-PARTY PRODUCTS 
The widespread use of customized vendor and other third-party products—including 
data, parameter values, or complete models—can present unique challenges for validation and 
other model risk management activities. Additionally, because certain components may be 
proprietary, banking organizations may not receive from the vendor the underlying code, data, or 
methodology that they would have if a model were developed internally. Nevertheless, the 
principles of model risk management remain applicable. 
An important element of model risk management is the validation of vendor products, 
either by internal or outside parties. Sound practice includes developing an understanding of the

12  
vendor model, including its conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance. 
Similarly, sound practice involves conducting ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis to 
assess whether vendor models are accurate, remain fit for purpose, and continue to be reliable. 
Such analysis can also be used to support any overlay or adjustment to model output. In cases 
where vendor models are customized to fit a banking organization’s specific business needs, 
sound practice also involves appropriately documenting, justifying, and evaluating adjustments 
made to customize the model as part of model validation.

### FDA 21 CFR Part 820

**820.75 Process validation.**
§ 820.75 Process validation.
============================

(a) Where the results of a process cannot be fully verified by subsequent inspection and test, the process shall be validated with a high degree of assurance and approved according to established procedures. The validation activities and results, including the date and signature of the individual(s) approving the validation and where appropriate the major equipment validated, shall be documented.

(b) Each manufacturer shall establish and maintain procedures for monitoring and control of process parameters for validated processes to ensure that the specified requirements continue to be met.

(1) Each manufacturer shall ensure that validated processes are performed by qualified individual(s).

(2) For validated processes, the monitoring and control methods and data, the date performed, and, where appropriate, the individual(s) performing the process or the major equipment used shall be documented.

(c) When changes or process deviations occur, the manufacturer shall review and evaluate the process and perform revalidation where appropriate. These activities shall be documented.
